title: Computational thinking, algorithms and data representation

questions.stem: The American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) is a character encoding standard adopted by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) in 1963.

parts.q: Why are encoding standards such as ASCII important?
parts.ask: Explain why a shared character encoding standard matters.

points.text: Allows data to be encoded in a standard way (every computer uses the same code for each character)
Provides a means of representing data as information
Allows for worldwide communication in electronic form

parts.scheme: Any one point: good description 3, fair 2. Allows data to be encoded in a standard way; provides a means of representing data as information; allows for worldwide communication in electronic form, or similar.
parts.model: Standards like ASCII mean every computer uses the same binary code for each character, so text created on one device is read correctly on any other. This allows data to be exchanged and communicated electronically worldwide.

idea.title: Character encoding
idea.text: Computers only store numbers, so a character set gives every character a number code (in ASCII, 'A' is 65). If everyone uses the same table, text saved or sent by one computer appears as the same text on another.

steps.say: Computers store everything as binary numbers, so each letter or symbol must be given a number code.
If two computers used different codes, the same binary would show up as different characters and the text would be garbled.
A standard means everyone agrees on the same codes, so text can be shared and communicated between any devices, worldwide.

parts.tip: Give both halves: the same codes everywhere, and what that allows (sharing text between different computers).

parts.q: State one limitation of ASCII.
parts.ask: Give one thing ASCII cannot do.

points.text: 7 bits, so only a maximum of 2^7 = 128 characters (accept 8 bits, 256 characters)
Does not allow for emojis
Does not support symbols from different languages / not enough symbols for languages with large character sets

parts.scheme: Good description 2, fair 1: 7 bits so only a maximum of 2^7 = 128 characters, 94 printable (accept 8 bits, max 256 characters); does not allow for emojis; does not support symbols from different languages; not enough symbols for languages with large character sets; and similar.
parts.model: ASCII uses only 7 bits, so it can represent at most 128 characters: not enough for the letters of other languages or for emojis.

idea.title: How many characters fit
idea.text: With n bits you can make 2^n different codes. ASCII's 7 bits give 128 codes: enough for English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes, but nothing more.

steps.say: Count ASCII's codes: 7 bits give 2^7 combinations.
128 is enough for English letters, digits and punctuation, but not for accented letters, other alphabets (Chinese, Arabic, Greek...) or emojis.
State one of these as the limitation, with the reason: only 128 characters.

parts.tip: Unicode was created to fix exactly this limitation.

idea.title: How bubble sort works
idea.text: Bubble sort compares neighbouring pairs from left to right and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After each pass the largest unsorted number has 'bubbled' to its final place at the end, so each pass needs one comparison fewer.

steps.say: Pass 2 starts with 5 8 7 6 9. The 9 is already in place, so there are 3 comparisons; the first (5 and 8, no swap) is given.
Compare 8 and 7: swap, giving 5 7 8 6 9. Compare 8 and 6: swap, giving 5 7 6 8 9. Now the 8 is in place too.
Pass 3 starts with 5 7 6 8 9 and needs 2 comparisons. 5 and 7: no swap, so the row stays 5 7 6 8 9. 7 and 6: swap, giving 5 6 7 8 9.
Pass 4 needs 1 comparison: 5 and 6 are in order, so the row is 5 6 7 8 9 and the list is sorted.

parts.tip: Write a row even when nothing is swapped (it repeats the row above): each row is one comparison and one mark.

questions.topic: Heuristics and the travelling salesperson problem
questions.stem:
The travelling salesperson problem is commonly used in the study of algorithms and appears in formats similar to the problem below.

“Given a list of cities and the distances between each pair of cities, what is the shortest possible route that visits each city once and returns to the original city?”
questions.fig: A map of six cities, city 1 marked Start/Finish, with road distances 1-2: 10, 1-3: 10, 1-4: 5, 2-3: 8, 2-5: 14, 3-5: 1, 3-4: 7, 3-6: 6, 5-6: 22, 4-6: 20.

parts.q: Why would heuristics be considered a good approach to solving a problem such as this?
parts.ask: Explain why heuristics suit the travelling salesperson problem.

points.text: Calculating the best actual solution (checking every route) would take too long
alts: too long|too much time|too slow|long time|ages|forever|impractical|infeasible|not feasible|unfeasible|years|centuries

points.text: A heuristic, a guess or rule of thumb based on experience, finds the best approximate solution

parts.scheme: Very good description 5, good 3, fair 1. Heuristics will find the best approximate solution when it would take too long to calculate the best actual solution, or similar. A heuristic is a guess which can be based on previous experience or a rule of thumb.
parts.model: To be sure of the shortest route you would have to check every possible route, and the number of routes grows so fast as cities are added that this would take far too long. A heuristic, a rule of thumb such as always travelling to the nearest unvisited city, finds a good approximate route quickly, which is usually good enough.

idea.title: What a heuristic is
idea.text: A heuristic is a rule of thumb or educated guess that finds a good answer quickly without guaranteeing the best one. It is used when the exact method would take far too long.

steps.say: The exact (brute force) method: list every route that starts and ends at city 1 and pick the shortest.
If every city were linked to every other, n cities would give (n − 1)!/2 different round trips, so the count explodes as cities are added.
Checking them all would take far too long for real problems, even on a fast computer.
A heuristic such as nearest neighbour (always go to the closest unvisited city) gives a good, near-shortest route very quickly: an approximate answer that is good enough.

parts.tip: Contrast the two: the exact solution takes too long; a heuristic gives a good approximate solution quickly.

questions.stem: In his book The Art of Computer Programming, Donald Knuth states that “searching is the most time-consuming part of many programs, and the substitution of a good search method for a bad one often leads to a substantial increase in speed.”
questions.fig: Photo of Donald Knuth; in (a) a Python search program; in (b)(ii) the sorted list L = [3, 7, 13, 18, 28, 35, 41, 50] (indexes 0-7) with left at index 0, mid at index 3 and right at index 7.

parts.q:
The Python code below shows an implementation of a search algorithm. Examine the code and answer the questions that follow:
```python
names = ["John", "Mary", "Zoe", "Alex", "Séamas"]
name = input("Enter lookup name: ")

found = False
index = 0

while (not found) and (index != len(names)):
    if name == names[index]:
        found = True
    else:
        index = index + 1

print("Result:", index)
```
State the name of the above search algorithm.
parts.ask: Name the search algorithm the code uses.
parts.scheme: Linear search: 2 marks.
parts.model: Linear search.

idea.title: Linear search
idea.text: A linear search checks the items one at a time from the start of the list until it finds the target or reaches the end. The list does not need to be sorted.

steps.say: Look at how index changes: it starts at 0 and goes up by 1 each time round the loop.
So each name is compared with the target in turn, first to last, until there is a match or the list runs out.
Checking the items one after another in order is a linear (sequential) search.

parts.q: What is the data type of the variable called found?
parts.ask: Give the data type of the variable found.
parts.scheme: Boole / Boolean 2 marks; True / False 1 mark.
parts.model: Boolean (bool).

idea.title: Boolean variables
idea.text: A Boolean variable holds one of only two values, True or False. Here found is a flag recording whether the name has been found yet.

steps.say: Look at the values found is given: False at the start and True when the name matches.
A variable that can only be True or False is a Boolean (bool in Python).

parts.tip: 'True/False' on its own earned only 1 mark: name the type, Boolean.

parts.q: Step through how the algorithm finds the name Zoe in the list called names.
parts.ask: Trace the loop step by step until it finds Zoe.

points.text: Starts at index 0: compares the first name, John; found stays False, index increased by 1
Index 1: compares the second name, Mary; found stays False, index increased to 2
Index 2: compares the third name, Zoe; found changes to True
Exits the while loop and prints the index, 2

parts.scheme: Very good description 5, good 3, fair 1: starts at index 0, compares John, found stays False; index increased by 1, compares Mary, found stays False; index increased by 1, compares Zoe, found changes to True; exits the while loop and prints index 2. Or any similar relevant explanation.
parts.model: index = 0: names[0] is John, not Zoe, so found stays False and index becomes 1. index = 1: Mary is not Zoe, so index becomes 2. index = 2: names[2] is Zoe, a match, so found becomes True. not found is now False, so the loop ends and it prints Result: 2.

idea.title: The loop condition
idea.text: The while loop keeps going only while found is False and index has not reached the end of the list. Setting found to True stops the loop.

steps.say: Start: found = False, index = 0. The loop condition is True, so the loop runs.
names[0] is "John", not "Zoe": the else branch runs and index becomes 1.
names[1] is "Mary", not "Zoe": index becomes 2.
names[2] is "Zoe": a match, so found = True (index stays 2).
not found is now False, so the loop stops and the program prints Result: 2.

parts.tip: Give index and found at every comparison: a step-by-step trace earns full marks, a one-line summary does not.

parts.q: What would be the value of index after running the algorithm if the user entered a name that was not present in the list called names?
parts.ask: Give index's final value when the name is not in the list.
parts.scheme: Index = 5: 2 marks.
parts.model: index = 5

steps.say: If the name never matches, found stays False and the else branch runs for every name.
index goes up by 1 after each of the 5 names.
When index = 5 = len(names), the condition index != len(names) is False, so the loop stops with index = 5.

parts.tip: 5 is one past the last valid index (4), so it signals 'not found'.

parts.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of this search algorithm? Explain your answer.
parts.ask: State linear search's worst-case complexity and explain why.

points.text: Worst case: O(n) / proportional to the length of the list
alts: o(n)|o( n )|big o of n|order n|order of n

points.text: Worst case is when the item is not in the list (or last), so each of the n items is checked: at most n comparisons
alts: n comparison|n checks|n steps|n items|n times|n elements|n names

parts.scheme: Answer O(n) / length of list 1 mark. Explanation (good 2, fair 1): the worst case means the item is not in the list, so each item is searched before it is found or not found; in a list of n items there would be at most n comparisons.
parts.model: O(n). In the worst case the name is not in the list (or is the last one), so the loop has to compare it with every one of the n names: n comparisons, so the time grows in direct proportion to the length of the list.

idea.title: Big O notation
idea.text: Big O describes how the number of steps grows as the input size n grows. O(n) means the work grows in direct proportion to n: double the list, double the comparisons.

steps.say: The worst case is the input that makes the algorithm do the most work.
For a linear search that is a name that is not in the list (or is the last one): every item must be checked.
A list of n items then needs n comparisons, so the time is proportional to n.

parts.tip: 1 mark is for O(n) and 2 for the explanation: say what the worst case is and why it needs n comparisons.

parts.q:
Binary search is generally regarded as a highly efficient search algorithm.

State one disadvantage of the binary search algorithm.
parts.ask: Give one drawback of binary search.

points.text: The data set must be sorted and remain sorted
Can be slower than linear search
More complicated than linear search and unnecessary for small data sets
Only works on data with a 'less-than' relationship / data has to be of the same type

parts.scheme: Any suitable answer, 2 marks: the data must be sorted and remain sorted; can be slower than linear search; more complicated and unnecessary for small data sets; only works on data with a 'less-than' relationship; data has to be of the same type.
parts.model: The list must already be sorted (and kept sorted) for binary search to work.

idea.title: Why binary search needs sorted data
idea.text: Binary search looks at the middle item and throws away the half that cannot contain the target. That only works if the list is in order, so it knows which half the target must be in.

steps.say: Recall how binary search chooses a half: if the target is bigger than the middle item, it must be to the right.
That reasoning is only true if the list is sorted.
So a disadvantage: the data must be sorted first (and kept sorted), which costs extra time.

parts.q:
Step through how the binary search algorithm finds the integer 28 in the list L shown below.
```
index  0   1   2    3    4    5    6    7
L      3   7   13   18   28   35   41   50
       ^             ^                   ^
       left          mid                 right
```
parts.ask: Trace binary search for 28, giving left, mid and right at each step.

points.text: Compares 28 with the value at mid (18): it is greater, so the left subarray is dismissed (left = 4)
Compares 28 with the new mid value (35, or 41 depending on the implementation): it is smaller, so the right subarray is dismissed
Compares 28 with mid (index 4): equal, found; returns index 4

parts.scheme: Very good description 5, good 3, fair 1. 28 > 18 (mid) so the left subarray is dismissed: left = 4, mid = 5 (35; mid may also be 41 depending on implementation, no deduction), right = 7. 28 < 35 so the right subarray is dismissed: right = 4, mid = 4. L[4] = 28: found, returns index 4. A left/mid/right/L[mid] table (0 3 7 18; 4 5 7 35; 4 4 4 28) is also accepted.
parts.model: Step 1: left = 0, right = 7, mid = 3, L[3] = 18. 28 > 18, so discard the left half: left = 4. Step 2: mid = (4 + 7) // 2 = 5, L[5] = 35. 28 < 35, so discard the right half: right = 4. Step 3: mid = (4 + 4) // 2 = 4, L[4] = 28: found at index 4.

idea.title: Binary search
idea.text: Binary search repeatedly checks the middle item of the part of the list still in play. If the target is bigger it keeps the right half, if smaller the left half, halving the search area each time until the target is found or nothing is left.

steps.say: Start: left = 0, right = 7, so mid = 3 and L[3] = 18.
28 > 18, so 28 must be to the right: left = mid + 1 = 4. New mid = 5 and L[5] = 35.
28 < 35, so 28 must be to the left: right = mid − 1 = 4. New mid = 4 and L[4] = 28.
L[4] = 28 matches, so the search stops: 28 is at index 4, found in 3 comparisons.

parts.tip: A small table of left, mid, right and L[mid] for each step is the clearest answer; rounding mid up (to 41) was also accepted.

parts.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons the binary search algorithm would need to make if the value to be searched for did not exist in a list of 8 items?
parts.ask: Find the most comparisons binary search makes on 8 items (value absent).
parts.scheme: 4: correct answer 2 marks; any relevant rough work 1 mark.

idea.title: Halving the list
idea.text: Each comparison halves the number of items still to be searched. A list of 8 items halves 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, and the last single item still needs a comparison.

steps.say: Each comparison discards about half of the items left (plus the middle one just checked).
Worst case, the larger part is kept each time: 8 items, then 4, then 2, then 1, with one comparison at each size.
That is 4 comparisons before nothing is left and the search reports 'not found'.

parts.tip: Try it on L: searching for 60 compares with 18, 35, 41 and 50, then stops: 4 comparisons.

parts.q: Why is the study of algorithmic efficiency considered to be important in computer science?
parts.ask: Explain why it matters to study how efficient algorithms are.

points.text: It allows different algorithms to be compared on time and efficiency
This matters particularly as data sets grow
It allows the best algorithm to be selected for the problem: the fastest and/or using the least memory

parts.scheme: Very good description 7, good 5, fair 3. It is important to understand the time and efficiency so that different algorithms can be compared, particularly as data sets grow; it allows the best algorithm to be selected for the specific problem; the best algorithm should be the fastest and/or use the least amount of memory.
parts.model: Studying efficiency lets us compare different algorithms for the same problem by how their running time and memory use grow with the size of the input. This matters most for large data sets, where an inefficient algorithm such as an O(n) linear search can be vastly slower than an O(log n) binary search. It lets programmers select the best algorithm for the problem: the one that is fastest and uses the least memory.

idea.title: Algorithmic efficiency
idea.text: Efficiency is how much time (number of steps) and memory an algorithm needs as its input grows. Two correct algorithms can differ hugely: on a million sorted items a linear search may need a million comparisons, a binary search about 20.

steps.say: Start from Knuth's point: swapping a bad method for a good one gives a big speed-up, so we need a way to tell which is better.
Efficiency analysis (such as Big O) compares algorithms by how their time and memory grow as the data grows.
Give an example: for 1,000,000 items, linear search needs up to 1,000,000 comparisons but binary search only about 20.
This lets us choose the best algorithm for a problem, the fastest and the one using the least memory, which matters most for large data sets.

parts.tip: A 7-mark answer needs several developed points: comparing algorithms, large data sets, and choosing the fastest/least-memory option, with an example.

idea.text: A trace table records the value of each variable after every step, so you can follow exactly what an algorithm does. Work through the flowchart box by box and write each new value in.

steps.say: Start: count, total and n are all 0 (the first row). count < 3 is TRUE, so go into the loop.
INPUT n = 7, then total = 0 + 7 = 7 and count = 0 + 1 = 1.
count = 1 < 3: INPUT n = 3, total = 7 + 3 = 10, count = 2.

parts.q: What output does the algorithm display?

The output box prints total/count.
So it displays 6, the average of 7, 3 and 8.

questions.stem: The Unicode representation for the ‘thumbs up’ emoji character, shown in Figure 2, is the hexadecimal number 1F44D.
questions.fig: Figure 2: the thumbs up emoji; in (b) 1F44D with an arrow to a row of 20 bit boxes, the first four filled in as 0001.

parts.q: Explain why emoji characters are not represented using the American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII).
parts.ask: Explain why ASCII cannot be used for emojis.

points.text: ASCII is a 7-bit system and cannot represent more than 128 characters (256 in extended ASCII)
ASCII was designed in the 1960s for the characters used then; emojis had not been invented
Emoji characters are represented using Unicode

parts.scheme: Good explanation 2: ASCII is a 7-bit system and cannot represent more than 128 characters (extended ASCII 256); it was published in 1963 with the characters commonly used then (digits, English letters, punctuation, control codes); emojis were not invented then so were not considered; emojis are represented using Unicode.
parts.model: ASCII uses only 7 bits, so it has room for just 128 characters (256 in extended ASCII), all chosen in the 1960s for English text and control codes, long before emojis existed. Emojis need many more codes, so they are encoded in Unicode.

idea.title: ASCII and Unicode
idea.text: ASCII has 128 codes for English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters. Unicode gives a unique code to over a million possible characters, covering every writing system and emojis.

steps.say: Count ASCII's capacity: 7 bits give 128 codes.
Those codes were all used in 1963 for English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes; emojis did not exist then.
The thumbs up's code, 1F44D, is 128077 in denary, far beyond ASCII's top code of 127, so it needs Unicode.

parts.q: Express the hexadecimal number 1F44D as a binary number. The first four bits have been completed for you.
parts.ask: Convert 1F44D to binary, four bits for each hex digit.
parts.scheme: 0001 1111 0100 0100 1101. Correct 3, half correct 2, response with some merit 1.

idea.title: Hex to binary
idea.text: Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so convert each digit on its own into a 4-bit group and write the groups side by side in the same order.

steps.say: Write each hex digit's denary value: 1, F = 15, 4, 4, D = 13.
Convert each to 4 bits using the place values 8, 4, 2, 1.
Join the groups in order.

parts.tip: Keep all four bits in every group (4 is 0100, not 100), or the digits shift and the answer is wrong.

questions.stem:
Consider a two-player game in which each player takes alternate turns at removing matchsticks from a board. The rules of the game are simple:
- at each turn a player must remove either one or two matchsticks
- the player who takes the last matchstick wins

Winning and losing positions are defined in terms of the number of matchsticks left on the board.

A winning position (W) is a position from which a player cannot lose if she/he makes all the optimal moves until the end of the game. For example, 2 is a winning position because if the player whose turn it is, makes the optimal move (i.e. removes the two remaining matchsticks) they will win that game.

A losing position (L) is a position from which a player cannot win (assuming that their opponent makes all the optimal moves until the game is over).

The win/loss table below depicts winning and losing positions for the scenarios where there are 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 matchsticks left on the board.

No. of matchsticks remaining: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Position (W or L): L, W, W, L, W
questions.fig: Photo of a pile of matchsticks; win/loss tables for 0-4 (L W W L W), 0-6 and 0-9 matchsticks; in (b)(i) a game tree from state (1, 2) with the AX1 branch complete.

parts.q: Explain why 3 is a losing position.
parts.ask: Show that every move from 3 leaves the opponent winning.

points.text: The only options are to take 1 or 2; taking 1 leaves 2 and taking 2 leaves 1, both winning positions for the opponent

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 2: the only options are to take 1 or 2 matchsticks and both leave the opponent in a winning position: taking 1 leaves 2 (the opponent takes both and wins); taking 2 leaves 1, also a winning position for the opponent.
parts.model: From 3 you must take 1 or 2. Taking 1 leaves 2 and taking 2 leaves 1, and both 2 and 1 are winning positions for your opponent, who just takes the rest. Every move loses, so 3 is a losing position.

idea.title: Winning and losing positions
idea.text: A position is losing if every possible move leaves the opponent in a winning position. It is winning if at least one move leaves the opponent in a losing position.

steps.say: List the moves from 3: take 1 (leaving 2) or take 2 (leaving 1).
Look both up in the table: 2 is W and 1 is W, and it is now the opponent's turn.
Every move hands the opponent a winning position, so 3 is L.

parts.q: Explain why 4 is a winning position.
parts.ask: Find a move from 4 that leaves the opponent losing.

points.text: The player can take 1 matchstick to leave the opponent with 3, a losing position

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 2: 4 is a winning position because the player can take 1 matchstick to leave the opponent with 3, which is a losing position (part (i)).
parts.model: From 4, take 1 matchstick. That leaves your opponent with 3, which is a losing position (part (i)), so you can force a win.

steps.say: Moves from 4: take 1 (leaving 3) or take 2 (leaving 2).
3 is L for the opponent, so taking 1 is a winning move.
One move to an L position is enough to make 4 a W.

parts.q: Calculate whether 5 and 6 are winning or losing positions and place your answers in the table below.
parts.ask: Work out W or L for 5 and 6 matchsticks.
parts.scheme: 5: W (taking two leaves the next player in a losing position); 6: L (any move, take 1 or 2, leaves the next player in a winning position). Each correct response 1 mark.
parts.model: 5 is W: take 2 to leave 3 (L). 6 is L: taking 1 leaves 5 (W) and taking 2 leaves 4 (W).

steps.say: 5: taking 2 leaves 3, which is L for the opponent, so 5 is W.
6: taking 1 leaves 5 (W) and taking 2 leaves 4 (W). Every move gives the opponent a W, so 6 is L.
The pattern so far: L at 0, 3 and 6, the multiples of 3.

parts.q: Assume you are about to start a new game with 21 matchsticks. If your opponent offered you the choice of going first or second, which would you choose? Justify your answer.
parts.ask: Decide whether to go first or second with 21 and justify it.

points.text: Decision: ask the opponent to go first (go second)
Reason: all multiples of 3 are losing positions, and 21 is a multiple of 3

parts.scheme: Correct decision 1 mark: ask the opponent to go first (go second). Justification 1 mark: 0, 3, 6, 9 etc. are losing positions; all multiples of 3 are losing positions, and 21 is a multiple of 3, so it is a losing position.
parts.model: I would go second. The losing positions are the multiples of 3 (0, 3, 6, 9, ...), and 21 = 3 × 7 is a multiple of 3, so whoever moves first from 21 is in a losing position if the other player plays well.

steps.say: Extend the pattern: the losing positions are 0, 3, 6, 9, ..., the multiples of 3.
21 = 3 × 7, so 21 is a losing position for the player about to move.
So let the opponent go first, then always take enough to leave them a multiple of 3.

parts.q: What strategy would you recommend in a game that started off with 20 matchsticks? Justify your answer.
parts.ask: Give a winning strategy for a 20-matchstick game and justify it.

points.text: Leave the opponent a multiple of 3 every turn: take 2 first (leaving 18), then take the opposite number to the opponent (they take 1, take 2; they take 2, take 1)
alts: opposite|3 minus|add up to 3|adds up to 3|total of 3|make 3|makes 3|sum to 3|add to 3|adds to 3

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 2: leave the opponent with a multiple of 3 matchsticks on every turn, so start by taking 2 (leaving 18), then for the rest of the game take the opposite number to the opponent: if they take 1, take 2; if they take 2, take 1.
parts.model: Go first and take 2, leaving 18, a multiple of 3. After that always take the opposite of your opponent (if they take 1, take 2; if they take 2, take 1), so each round removes 3 and they always face a multiple of 3, a losing position.

steps.say: 20 is not a multiple of 3, so it is a winning position for the player who moves first.
Take 2 to leave 18 = 3 × 6, a losing position for the opponent.
Then each turn take 3 minus what they took, so together you remove 3 every round and they always face a multiple of 3, all the way down to 0.

parts.q:
Consider a variation of the game described in part (a) with two key differences: the matchsticks are initially arranged into two separate piles on the board and a player can remove any number of matchsticks from a single pile on their go. We will call the two piles pile X and pile Y.

For example, in a game where pile X contains 10 matchsticks and pile Y contains 9 matchsticks, a player may decide to remove 9 matchsticks from pile Y on their go.

The player who removes the last matchstick(s) wins the game.

Below is a partially completed diagram for an end game scenario in which it is player A’s turn and there is only one matchstick left in pile X and two matchsticks left in pile Y (denoted by 1, 2).

The purpose of the diagram is to depict the eventual outcome for every possible move from this point in the game. The left-hand branch of the diagram has been completed covering all eventualities if player A removes 1 matchstick from pile X (denoted by AX1).

Complete the diagram to illustrate all possible moves and show who wins in each case.
parts.ask: Complete the game tree from (1, 2): the state after each move and the winner.
parts.scheme: Full correct solution 5 marks: AY1 → (1, 1), then BX1 → (0, 1), AY1 → (0, 0) player A wins, or BY1 → (1, 0), AX1 → (0, 0) player A wins; AY2 → (1, 0), BX1 → (0, 0) player B wins. Otherwise 2 marks for the 1st full correct path, 2 for the 2nd, 1 for the 3rd (or 1 mark for correct pairs in a path).

idea.title: Game trees
idea.text: A game tree shows every possible move from a position as a branch and every resulting position as a node, until each game ends. Reading the end of each path tells you who wins down that path.

steps.say: From (1, 2), A's other moves take from pile Y: AY1 leaves (1, 1) and AY2 leaves (1, 0).
From (1, 1), B can play BX1 → (0, 1) or BY1 → (1, 0). Either way A takes the last matchstick (AY1 or AX1) → (0, 0): A wins.
From (1, 0), B's only move is BX1 → (0, 0): B takes the last matchstick and wins.

parts.tip: Keep the (X, Y) notation and label every arrow with the player, the pile and the number taken, like the given branch.

parts.q: Based on the completed diagram which is player A’s best move? Why?

points.text: It is the only move that leads to certain victory for A

parts.scheme: Best move AY1, 1 mark; reason 1 mark: it is the only move that leads to certain victory for A.
parts.model: Player A’s best move: AY1. Reason: it leaves (1, 1), and whichever matchstick B takes, A takes the last one, so it is the only move that guarantees A wins.

steps.say: Check each of A's first moves on the tree.
AX1 can lose (if B plays BY2) and AY2 always loses (B plays BX1).
After AY1, both of B's moves lead to A winning, so AY1 is the only move that guarantees victory.

parts.model: Take 1 matchstick from pile Y (AY1), leaving (2, 2). If B then takes a whole pile, A takes the other pile and wins; if B takes 1, leaving (1, 2) or (2, 1), A wins as shown in part (ii).

steps.say: Look for a move that leaves the opponent equal piles: from (2, 3), take 1 from Y to leave (2, 2).
Check B's replies: if B takes 2 from a pile, A takes the other pile and wins; if B takes 1, the state is (1, 2) or (2, 1), which A wins by the tree in parts (i) and (ii).
So AY1 is a winning move.

parts.q: Hence, or otherwise, describe a winning strategy from state $(n, m)$, where $n \neq m$.
parts.ask: Describe a winning strategy from two unequal piles.

points.text: Even the piles: leave (n, n) or (m, m); for m > n take m − n matchsticks, for m < n take n − m

parts.scheme: Very good description 2: even the piles, leaving (n, n) or (m, m): for m > n take m − n matchsticks; for m < n take n − m.
parts.model: Take the difference between the piles from the bigger pile (m − n matchsticks if m > n) so the piles are equal. Then after every move by the opponent, make the same move on the other pile so the piles stay equal; you will take the last matchstick.

steps.say: Parts (ii) and (iii) show that leaving equal piles puts the opponent in a losing position.
If m > n, take m − n from the bigger pile to leave (n, n).
math: (n, m) \to (n, n) \text{ by taking } m - n

steps.say: Then mirror the opponent: whatever they take from one pile, take the same from the other, so the piles stay equal until you take the last matchstick.

parts.q: Explain why $(n, n, n)$ is a winning position in a game where 3 piles are used?

points.text: Remove one of the piles, leaving (n, n), equal piles

parts.scheme: Very good description 2: since (n, n) is the position to leave the opponent, a winning strategy would be to remove one of the piles.
parts.model: The player to move removes one whole pile, leaving two equal piles (n, n). By part (iv), equal piles are a losing position for the opponent: whatever they take from one pile, you take the same from the other, so you take the last matchstick.

steps.say: From (n, n, n), you may take any number from one pile, including the whole pile.
Take a whole pile: the opponent faces (n, n), two equal piles.
From equal piles the mirroring strategy of part (iv) wins for you, so (n, n, n) is a winning position.

parts.ask: Explain how one computational thinking skill helped solve the game.

points.text: Abstraction: ignoring other details to focus on one, and using representations for physical objects/actions: (1, 2) for the piles, A and B for players, AX1 for a move, win/loss tables and tree diagrams
Decomposition: breaking the problem down to work out every possible outcome, e.g. starting from 0 matchsticks (a losing position) and building up a winning strategy
Pattern recognition: seeing that multiples of 3 are losing positions, or that keeping both piles equal wins, and generalising to a strategy

Decomposition: breaking the problem down to work out every outcome; starting from zero matchsticks as a losing position and building up a strategy. questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows a row of black and white discs with their position numbers shown under each square. There are only two ways to move a disc:
1. Move into an empty square one position to the left or right, for example 1 → 2 means move the disc from square 1 to square 2.
2. Jump in either direction over a single adjacent disc into an empty space immediately beyond, for example 3 → 1 means move the disc from square 3 to square 1, jumping over a disc in square 2.
questions.fig: Figure 1 (start state): five squares numbered 0 to 4 holding white, white, empty, black, black. Figure 2 (end state): black, black, empty, white, white.

parts.q: Write a sequence of steps, or an algorithm, that swaps all the white discs with the black discs so that the row looks like that shown in Figure 2. You can only move a single disc in each step.
parts.ask: List the moves (from → to) that swap the white and black discs
parts.scheme: Full correct solution 6 marks, e.g. 1→2, 3→1, 4→3, 2→4, 0→2, 1→0, 3→1, 2→3; four or more correct steps in the correct order 4 marks; a response with some merit 2 marks.

idea.title: A sequence of moves
idea.text: A puzzle like this is solved by an algorithm: a sequence of legal moves from the start state to the end state. The trick is to keep the colours alternating, so a disc always has an empty square to slide into or jump to.

steps.say: Start: W W _ B B. Slide a white disc into the gap: 1→2 gives W _ W B B.
A black disc jumps over the white one into the gap: 3→1 gives W B W _ B. Then 4→3 slides the other black disc: W B W B _.
Now the whites jump right over the blacks: 2→4 gives W B _ B W, and 0→2 gives _ B W B W.
The blacks move left: 1→0 slides (B _ W B W), then 3→1 jumps (B B W _ W).
Last, 2→3 slides the white disc: B B _ W W, which is Figure 2. That is 8 moves.

parts.tip: Write each move in the paper's own from → to format and check the row after every move. The mirror solution, starting 3→2, is just as good.

LOOP until problem_solved IS TRUE

```

idea.title: The input symbol
idea.text: In a flowchart a parallelogram is an input or output step. The variables named in the input parallelogram are the ones whose values are read in.

steps.say: Find the parallelogram near the top of the flowchart: it says a, b ← INPUT.
The variables given their values by INPUT are the input variables: a and b.
t is not an input: it gets its value inside the algorithm (t ← a).

parts.q: Explain the purpose of the variable t.
parts.ask: Explain why the flowchart needs the variable t

points.text: t is a temporary variable used to store the value of a
Without t, the contents of a would be lost when b is assigned to a

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 3 marks, fair 2: t is a temporary variable used to store the value of a; without t the contents of a would be lost when b is assigned to a.
parts.model: t is a temporary variable that holds a copy of a's value, so that when a is overwritten by b (a ← b) the original value of a is not lost and can then be put into b (b ← t).

idea.title: The temporary swap
idea.text: Assigning a ← b overwrites a, so its old value would be gone for good. Saving it first in a temporary variable lets you finish the swap.

steps.say: Try the swap without t: if a = 3 and b = 5, a ← b makes a = 5, then b ← a makes b = 5 as well. The 3 is lost.
steps.code:

b ← a   # b = 5, the 3 is gone

steps.say: With t, t ← a keeps a copy of the 3 before a is overwritten.
steps.code:

a ← b   # a = 5
b ← t   # b = 3

steps.say: So t is a temporary store that stops a's value being lost during the swap.

The Python code below shows an implementation of the bubble sort algorithm.

    for j in range(len(values)-1):

            t = values[j+1]
            values[j+1] = values[j]
            values[j] = t

print("OUTPUT:", values)
```

parts.q:
The algorithm takes five passes to complete the bubble sort of the integers in values.

Apply the bubble sort algorithm to sort values. Show the contents of values after each of the five passes.
parts.ask: Fill in values after each of the five bubble sort passes
parts.model: After pass 1: 50 30 60 20 70. After pass 2: 30 50 20 60 70. After pass 3: 30 20 50 60 70. After pass 4: 20 30 50 60 70. After pass 5: 20 30 50 60 70.

idea.title: Bubble sort passes
idea.text: One pass compares each neighbouring pair from left to right and swaps them if the left one is bigger. Each pass carries the biggest unsorted value to the end of the list.

steps.say: Pass 1 on 50 70 30 60 20: 50 and 70 stay; 70 and 30 swap; 70 and 60 swap; 70 and 20 swap.
Pass 2: 50 and 30 swap; 50 and 60 stay; 60 and 20 swap; 60 and 70 stay.
Pass 3: 30 and 50 stay; 50 and 20 swap; the rest stay.
Pass 4: 30 and 20 swap and nothing else moves, so the list is now sorted.
Pass 5 still runs (the code always makes 5 passes) but makes no swaps, so the row is the same: 20 30 50 60 70.

parts.tip: Pass 5 is the same as pass 4: the code doesn't stop early, so still write that row out.

parts.q: The bubble sort algorithm has O($n^2$) best and worst case time complexity. Explain what this means in terms of the number of compare operations performed.
parts.ask: Explain what O(n²) means for bubble sort's number of comparisons

points.text: In a list of size N bubble sort performs N passes, each with N − 1 compares: N² − N in total, which for large N is about N²
The best case (already sorted) and the worst case (reverse order) carry out the same number of comparisons
As the number of elements increases the compares increase quadratically: a list of 5 needs about 25, and doubling the list increases them about four times

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 5 marks, good 3, fair 1. A list of N items gets N passes of N − 1 compares, N² − N in all, about N² for large N; the best case (already sorted) and the worst case (reverse order) make the same number of compares; the compares grow quadratically, so a list of 5 needs about 25 and doubling the list's size could make four times as many.
parts.model: For a list of n items the algorithm makes n passes with n − 1 comparisons in each, so n² − n comparisons, which is about n² for large n. It makes this many whether the list is already sorted (best case) or in reverse order (worst case), so doubling the length of the list roughly quadruples the number of comparisons.

idea.title: Big O counts growth
idea.text: O(n²) means the work grows with the square of the input's size. Bubble sort compares every neighbouring pair on every pass, so doubling n makes about four times as many compares.

steps.say: Count the compares in this code: the outer loop runs n times and the inner loop n − 1 times each time.
steps.code:
for i in range(len(values)):        # n passes
    for j in range(len(values)-1):  # n - 1 compares each

questions.stem: A binary question is a question that has two possible answers – yes or no. The diagrams, in Figure 1 and Figure 2 below, describe how binary questions can be chained together to determine the outcome of tossing a six-sided dice. Two different search algorithms are illustrated.
questions.fig: Figure 1 (Algorithm 1, tree depth = 5): a chain of questions 1? 2? 3? 4? 5?, where each Yes gives that number and each No goes on to the next question. Figure 2 (Algorithm 2, tree depth = 3): first >=4?, then 3? or 6?, then 2? or 5?, splitting the numbers in half each time.

parts.q: State the name of each search algorithm.
parts.ask: Name the search algorithm shown in each figure
parts.scheme: 1 mark each: Algorithm 1 is a linear search; Algorithm 2 is a binary search.
parts.model: Algorithm 1: linear search. Algorithm 2: binary search.

idea.title: Two ways to search
idea.text: A linear search checks the items one at a time from the start. A binary search compares with the middle and throws away half of the remaining items with every question.

steps.say: Figure 1 asks about each number in turn (1? 2? 3? ...) until it gets a yes: checking one item at a time is a linear search.
Figure 2 first asks >=4?, which splits the six numbers into two halves, then splits again: halving each time is a binary search.

parts.q: Suggest which of the two algorithms is most efficient. Justify your answer.
parts.ask: Pick the more efficient algorithm and justify your choice

points.text: In general binary search is more efficient: at worst it needs about log(n) operations, while linear search needs O(n)
Linear search may be more efficient: there is no sort overhead, the target is sometimes one of the first items, and for small lists it can beat binary search

parts.scheme: Very good justification 4 marks, fair 2. Either: binary search is in general more efficient, as at worst it needs only log(n) operations while linear search needs O(n); or: linear search may be more efficient, as there is no sort overhead, the target is sometimes one of the first items, and for small lists it can beat a binary search.
parts.model: Most efficient: Algorithm 2 (binary search). Justify: each question halves the numbers that are left, so it needs at most 3 questions (about log₂ n) to find the result, while the linear search can need 5, and that number grows in step with n.

idea.title: Halving beats stepping
idea.text: A linear search can take as many steps as there are items, O(n). A binary search halves what is left each time, so it takes only about log₂ n steps: 3 for 6 outcomes, 10 for 1,000.

steps.say: Worst case for Algorithm 1: the dice shows 5 or 6, which takes 5 questions (the tree depth).
Worst case for Algorithm 2: never more than 3 questions, because each question halves the numbers left.
So the binary search is more efficient here, and the gap grows with more items: O(log n) against O(n).
A linear search can win when the answer is one of the first items, the list is tiny or the data isn't sorted (no sort overhead): the scheme accepts that choice too if you justify it.

parts.q:
The Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of two integers a and b is the largest number that divides into both with no remainder. One of the oldest and most famous algorithms was first described by Greek mathematician, Euclid, in his book of Elements written around 300BC. The code snippet below is an implementation of Euclid’s algorithm using subtraction to find the GCD of 45 and 18.
```python
 1  def gcd(a, b):
 2      while a != b:
 3          if a > b:
 4              a = a - b
 5          elif b > a:
 6              b = b - a
 7
 8      return a
 9
10  print("The GCD is", gcd(45,18))
```
State the purpose of the def keyword on line 1 of the code.
parts.ask: Say what the def keyword does on line 1

points.text: To introduce (define) the function gcd

parts.scheme: 2 marks: it introduces (defines) the function gcd.
parts.model: def defines a function: it introduces a new function called gcd that takes the parameters a and b.

idea.title: Defining a function
idea.text: def tells Python that a function definition follows: its name, its parameters in brackets, then the indented body that runs each time the function is called.

steps.say: Read line 1: def gcd(a, b): has the keyword def, then a name, then the parameters.
def is the keyword that defines (creates) a function, here one named gcd with parameters a and b.
The function's body only runs when it is called, as on line 10: gcd(45,18).

parts.q: Starting from line 2 of the code, complete the trace table shown below. The variables a and b have been initialised to 45 and 18 respectively.
parts.ask: Trace a and b through the while loop until they are equal
parts.scheme: 1 mark for each correct row, 4 marks for a full correct response: 27, 18; 9, 18; 9, 9.

idea.title: Subtract the smaller
idea.text: Euclid's algorithm keeps replacing the bigger number with the difference of the two. Any common divisor of both also divides their difference, so when the two numbers become equal that number is the GCD.

steps.say: 45 != 18 and a > b, so line 4 runs: a = a − b.
27 != 18 and a > b again.
9 != 18, but now b > a, so line 6 runs: b = b − a.
Now a = b = 9, so the condition a != b is false, the loop stops and gcd returns 9.

parts.tip: Write a new row only when a value changes, and stop as soon as a equals b.

parts.q: This implementation uses a while loop. Explain why a for loop would not be suitable for this algorithm.
parts.ask: Explain why a for loop doesn't suit this algorithm

points.text: The number of iterations is not known in advance of running the algorithm
The number of iterations required can vary depending on the arguments passed into the function gcd

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 4 marks, fair 2: the number of iterations is not known before the algorithm runs; it can vary depending on the arguments passed into gcd.
parts.model: A for loop is used when the number of iterations is known in advance. Here we can't tell how many subtractions are needed until a and b become equal, as it depends on the values passed in, so a while loop that repeats until a == b is needed.

idea.title: Definite and indefinite loops
idea.text: A for loop repeats a fixed, known number of times (over a range or a list). A while loop repeats until a condition changes, which suits work where you can't tell in advance how many steps it will take.

steps.say: For 45 and 18 the loop ran 3 times; for 100 and 1 it would run 99 times.
So the number of iterations depends on a and b and isn't known before the loop starts.
A for loop needs that count up front; a while loop just keeps going until a != b becomes false, which is what this algorithm needs.

parts.q:
The code below shows a recursive implementation to find the GCD of two integers.
```python
 1  def recursive_gcd(a, b):
 2      if b == 0:
 3          return a
 4      return recursive_gcd(b, a%b)
 5
 6  print("The GCD is", recursive_gcd(45, 18))
```
Every recursive function, including the one shown here, has a base case and a recursive case. Outline the meaning of the terms ‘base case’ and ‘recursive case’.
parts.ask: Explain the terms 'base case' and 'recursive case'

points.text: The condition that stops the recursive function from calling itself indefinitely (or until a stack overflow error occurs)
The simplest version of the problem, whose answer is known, e.g. recursive_gcd(a, 0) is a
In the example code the condition b == 0 is the base case
alts: b == 0|b==0|b is 0|b is zero|b = 0|b equals 0|b equals zero

points.text: The part of the function that calls itself to solve a simpler/smaller version of the problem
The recursive calls eventually converge on the base case

parts.scheme: 2 marks for each case (very good 2, fair 1). Base case: the condition that stops the function calling itself indefinitely (or until a stack overflow); the simplest version of the problem, whose answer is known, e.g. recursive_gcd(a, 0) is a; here b == 0. Recursive case: the part of the function that calls itself to solve a simpler or smaller version of the problem; the calls eventually converge on the base case; here recursive_gcd(b, a % b).
parts.model: Base case: the simplest case, which the function answers directly without calling itself, so the recursion stops; here, when b == 0 it returns a. Recursive case: the part where the function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem, here recursive_gcd(b, a%b), getting closer to the base case each time.

idea.title: Recursion
idea.text: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it. The base case is the version small enough to answer straight away, and it stops the chain of calls.

steps.say: Lines 2 and 3 are the base case: if b == 0 the answer is simply a, returned with no further call.
Line 4 is the recursive case: the function calls itself with smaller values, (b, a%b).
Each call gets closer to b = 0: (45, 18) → (18, 9) → (9, 0), which returns 9.
Without a base case the calls would never stop, and the program would crash with a stack overflow.

parts.q:
Explain the use of the variable b and the expression a%b on line 4 of the code.
```python
 4      return recursive_gcd(b, a%b)
```
parts.ask: Explain what b and a%b do in the call on line 4

points.text: b is the first argument (parameter/value) passed into the function, as a
Within the function b decides whether the base case (b == 0) is reached
a%b is the second argument (parameter/value) passed into the function, as b
It computes the remainder when a is divided by b; the remainder becomes the new value of b in the next recursive call
It reduces the problem size, as the GCD of a and b is the same as the GCD of b and a % b

parts.scheme: 3 marks for each (very good 3, fair 2). b: it is the first argument passed into the function, as a (and within the function b decides whether the base case b == 0 is reached). a%b: it is the second argument, passed in as b; it computes the remainder when a is divided by b, which becomes the new b in the next call, reducing the problem since the GCD of a and b equals the GCD of b and a%b.
parts.model: b: the current b is passed as the first argument, so it becomes the new a in the next call. a%b: the remainder when a is divided by b is passed as the second argument, so it becomes the new b; this makes the numbers smaller with each call until the remainder is 0, the base case.

idea.title: Remainders shrink it
idea.text: The GCD of a and b is also the GCD of b and the remainder a % b. Passing (b, a%b) gives a smaller pair every call, until the remainder is 0 and the GCD is left in a.

steps.say: a%b is the remainder of a ÷ b. For 45 and 18: 45 = 2 × 18 + 9, so 45 % 18 = 9.
Line 4 calls recursive_gcd(b, a%b): b goes into the first position, so the old b becomes the new a.
The remainder a%b goes into the second position, so it becomes the new b, which is smaller than before.
Trace: (45, 18) → (18, 9) → (9, 0). Now b == 0, the base case, so 9 is returned.

parts.q: Given a choice of using gcd shown in part (a), or recursive_gcd shown here in part (b), which version would you recommend to find the greatest common divisor of very large numbers on machines with limited RAM? Justify your answer, in terms of memory utilisation.
parts.ask: Choose gcd or recursive_gcd for a machine with little RAM, and justify it

points.text: The non-recursive solution avoids the potentially high memory overhead of recursion (and the possibility of a stack overflow)
In the non-recursive solution memory usage stays constant, as the loop reuses the same variables
In the recursive solution memory usage grows with each recursive call as the call stack increases, which could exhaust the stack for very large numbers

parts.scheme: 1 mark for gcd; justification very good 4 marks, fair 2: the non-recursive version avoids the memory overhead of recursion (and a possible stack overflow); its memory use stays constant because the loop reuses the same variables; in the recursive version memory use grows with every call as the call stack grows, and for very large numbers this could exhaust the stack.
parts.model: gcd or recursive_gcd: gcd. Justify: the while-loop version reuses the same two variables, so its memory use stays constant. Every call of recursive_gcd adds a new frame to the call stack, so memory use grows with the number of calls, and with very large numbers on a machine with little RAM it could run out of stack space (a stack overflow).

idea.title: The call stack
idea.text: Every function call that hasn't finished keeps a stack frame in memory with its own copies of its variables. A loop reuses the same variables; deep recursion piles up frames until memory runs out.

steps.say: gcd uses a while loop: the same two variables, a and b, are updated each time round, so its memory use doesn't grow.
recursive_gcd calls itself; each call waits for the next one to finish and keeps its own a and b on the call stack.
Very large numbers can need many calls, so the stack can grow until it runs out of memory: a stack overflow.
With limited RAM, recommend gcd, the iterative version.

parts.tip: Name your choice and justify it in terms of memory, as asked: constant memory against a growing call stack.

parts.q:
Quicksort is a widely used sorting algorithm developed by British computer scientist Tony Hoare in 1960. The algorithm itself is recursive and it uses a process called partitioning around a chosen pivot to achieve its objective. Quicksort is known for its efficiency and speed, especially in handling very long lists of data.

Given the unsorted list shown below and a pivot of 13, state the contents of the two sub-lists created after one partitioning step of quicksort.

29    10    14    37    13
parts.ask: Partition the list around the pivot 13 into two sub-lists
parts.scheme: 1 mark for each correct sub-list: left [10], right [29, 14, 37].
parts.model: Left sub-list: [10]. Right sub-list: [29, 14, 37].

idea.title: Partitioning
idea.text: Partitioning puts every item smaller than the pivot into a left sub-list and every item bigger (or equal) into a right sub-list. The pivot then sits between them, in its final position.

steps.say: Go through the list and compare each item with the pivot, 13.
29 > 13 goes right; 10 < 13 goes left; 14 > 13 goes right; 37 > 13 goes right.
Left sub-list: [10]. Right sub-list: [29, 14, 37], in their original order. The pivot sits between them: [10] 13 [29, 14, 37].

parts.tip: Leave the pivot out of both sub-lists: it is already in its final place.

parts.q: Describe the next steps quicksort would take in order to achieve its objective.
parts.ask: Describe what quicksort does after this first partition

points.text: Quicksort applies the same process (recursively) to each sub-list created by the partitioning
If a sub-list has only one element it is already sorted
For larger sub-lists a new pivot is chosen and the list is divided into elements less than the pivot and elements greater than or equal to it
Once all sub-lists are reduced to single elements they are combined in order, giving a fully sorted list

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 5 marks, good 3, fair 1 (an appropriate diagram is accepted): quicksort applies the same process to each sub-list; a sub-list of one element is already sorted; for a larger sub-list a new pivot is chosen and it is divided into elements less than the pivot and elements greater than or equal to it; this divide and conquer repeats recursively until all sub-lists are single elements, which are combined in order to give the fully sorted list.
parts.model: Quicksort now repeats the same process recursively on each sub-list. [10] has one element, so it is already sorted. For [29, 14, 37] a new pivot is chosen, e.g. 37, giving [29, 14] and []; then [29, 14] is partitioned with the pivot 14 into [] and [29]. When every sub-list has one element (or none) they are combined in order: [10, 13, 14, 29, 37].

idea.title: Divide and conquer
idea.text: Quicksort splits the problem into smaller sub-lists and sorts each one the same way. A list with zero or one items is already sorted, and that is where the recursion stops.

steps.say: After one partition the list is [10] 13 [29, 14, 37], with the pivot 13 in its final place.
[10] has only one item, so it is already sorted: nothing more to do there.
[29, 14, 37] gets a new pivot (say 37, the last item) and is partitioned: [29, 14] 37 [ ].
Repeat on [29, 14] with the pivot 14: [ ] 14 [29]. Every sub-list now has at most one item.
Put the pieces back together in order: 10, 13, 14, 29, 37.

parts.tip: A small diagram of the sub-lists splitting is accepted and makes the recursion easy to show.

parts.q: Outline two common strategies used when selecting a pivot for a quicksort algorithm.
parts.ask: Give two ways of choosing a quicksort pivot

points.text: First element
Last element
Middle element
Median of the first, middle and last element
Median of medians
Random element

parts.scheme: 1 mark for each correct strategy: first element, last element, middle element, median of the first, middle and last elements, median of medians, a random element.
parts.model: 1. Choose the last element of the list as the pivot. 2. Choose a random element as the pivot.

idea.title: Pivot choice matters
idea.text: Any element can be the pivot, but one near the median splits the list evenly and keeps quicksort fast. Simple rules take a fixed position; better ones take a random element or a median.

steps.say: The simplest strategies take a fixed position: the first, the last or the middle element.
Better strategies aim for a value near the median: a random element, or the median of the first, middle and last elements.
Write two, each in a few words: e.g. 'the last element of the list' and 'a random element'.

parts.q: Referring to Figure 4 below, explain the best and worst-case time complexity of the quicksort algorithm.
parts.ask: Explain quicksort's best and worst case, using the graph

points.text: O(n log n): each pivot divides the list evenly into two halves, giving a balanced recursion tree of about log n levels, with all n elements processed at each level
O(n²): the pivot repeatedly creates very unbalanced splits (it is always the smallest or largest element), so one sub-list has n − 1 elements and the other 0, giving n levels of n elements

parts.scheme: 2 marks for each case (very good 2, fair 1). Best case O(n log n): each pivot divides the list evenly into two halves, a balanced recursion tree about log n levels deep, with all n elements processed once at each level. Worst case O(n²): the pivot repeatedly makes very unbalanced splits (always the smallest or largest element), so one sub-list has n − 1 elements and the other 0, a tree n levels deep with n elements processed at each level; this can happen on sorted or reverse-sorted lists if no precautions are taken.
parts.model: Best case: O(n log n), the lower curve. Each pivot splits the list into two equal halves, so there are about log n levels of splitting and each level processes all n items. Worst case: O(n²), the steep curve. If the pivot is always the smallest or largest item (e.g. an already sorted list with the last item as pivot), each split only removes one item, so there are n levels of about n items each.

idea.title: Even splits are fast
idea.text: Quicksort's speed depends on how evenly each pivot splits the list. Even halves give about log n levels of work; lopsided splits give n levels, so the time grows like n².

steps.say: Each level of partitioning compares every item with a pivot: about n operations per level.
Best case: the pivot is the median each time, so the lists halve, and halving n items takes about log₂ n levels.
Worst case: the pivot is the smallest or largest item each time, so a split only removes one item and there are n levels.
On Figure 4, O(n log n) rises gently while O(n²) shoots up: for 1,000 items that is about 10,000 steps against 1,000,000.

parts.tip: Refer to the figure, as the question asks: say which curve is the best case and which the worst.

idea.text: In a model the input variables are the factors you feed in or change; the output variable is the result the model predicts from them.

idea.title: Pattern recognition
idea.text: Spotting a pattern means finding something that repeats in the data, such as an input value that keeps going with the same output. Patterns like these are what a model uses to make predictions.

idea.title: Better inputs, better model
idea.text: A model is only as good as the factors it includes. Adding variables that plausibly affect the result helps it predict more accurately.

parts.q:
The quote below is attributed to statistician George Box and is often cited in the context of modelling and simulation. It highlights the limitations of models while emphasising their practical value.

"All models are wrong, but some are useful"

Outline one limitation and one benefit of modelling and simulation.
parts.ask: Give one limitation and one benefit of modelling and simulation

points.text: Models are abstractions that simplify complex systems and omit many details, so they never fully represent reality
Underlying assumptions of the model may not always hold true
Data limitations (e.g. bias, errors, size) can make models inaccurate
Ethical concerns regarding privacy, security and accountability
High development costs
Models make complex systems easier to understand and identify patterns, relationships and areas for intervention
Models can provide valuable predictions within a defined scope
Models help decision-makers weigh options and test scenarios in a controlled, low-risk environment

parts.scheme: 2 marks for each (very good 2, fair 1). Limitations: models are abstractions that omit details, so are never fully accurate; their assumptions may not hold; data limitations (bias, errors, size); ethical concerns (privacy, security, accountability); high development costs. Benefits: they make complex systems easier to understand (patterns, relationships, where to intervene); valuable predictions within a defined scope; options and scenarios can be tested in a controlled, low-risk environment (e.g. a traffic flow simulation for city planners).
parts.model: Limitation: a model is a simplification that leaves out details of the real system, so its predictions are never exactly right. Benefit: different scenarios, like changing traffic-light timings, can be tested safely and cheaply on the model before being tried in the real world.

idea.title: Wrong but useful
idea.text: Every model leaves things out, so it can never match reality exactly: it is 'wrong'. But if it keeps the factors that matter, it can still explain and predict well enough to make decisions: it is 'useful'.

steps.say: 'Wrong' points to a limitation: models simplify, and their assumptions and data may be imperfect.
'Useful' points to a benefit: models let us understand, predict and test 'what if' scenarios safely and cheaply.
Write one of each, with a short reason or example.

parts.q: Explain why abstraction is important when developing a model.
parts.ask: Explain why abstraction matters when building a model

points.text: Abstraction allows us to focus on the most essential elements of a system while ignoring unnecessary details
By simplifying complex systems, abstraction makes it easier to understand, analyse and simulate the system's behaviour
Without abstraction, models would become too complicated, difficult to interpret and less effective in predicting outcomes or testing scenarios

parts.scheme: Very good explanation 4 marks, fair 2: abstraction lets you focus on the most essential elements of a system while ignoring unnecessary details; simplifying the system makes it easier to understand, analyse and simulate its behaviour; without it models would be too complicated, hard to interpret and less effective at predicting outcomes or testing scenarios.
parts.model: Abstraction means keeping only the details that matter and ignoring the rest. In the driving test model we keep age, transmission and instructor experience but not, say, the colour of the car. This keeps the model simple enough to understand, build and run, whereas including every detail would make it far too complicated to be useful.

idea.title: Abstraction
idea.text: Abstraction is a computational thinking skill: removing unnecessary detail so you can focus on what matters for the problem. A map is an abstraction of a city: it leaves most things out, and that is why it is useful.

steps.say: Start with the definition: abstraction removes unnecessary detail and keeps the essential features.
Why it matters for a model: a real system has endless details, and a model can't include them all.
Keeping only the key factors makes the model simple enough to understand, build, run and interpret.
Give an example: the driving test model keeps age and transmission but ignores the colour of the car.

parts.tip: Define abstraction, then say why it helps (simpler, easier to understand and run) for the full 4 marks.

parts.q:
Modelling and simulation can be used in many situations to address a wide variety of problems. Some example areas where modelling and simulation can be used to improve outcomes include:
- Education
- Mental wellbeing
- Environment
- Traffic management
Pick any two of the above areas and briefly describe how modelling could be used to address a problem and improve outcomes.
parts.ask: For two of the areas, describe how modelling could tackle a problem

points.text: Education: simulate different teaching methods or learning environments to find the most effective approaches for student engagement and performance (e.g. a virtual classroom)
Mental wellbeing: simulate factors like stress levels, social interactions and lifestyle choices to predict outcomes and suggest personalised interventions (e.g. identify triggers for anxiety)
Environment: simulate natural systems such as climate change or ecosystem dynamics to predict future conditions, guiding policy decisions and sustainable resource management
Traffic management: simulate the movement of vehicles in a city to identify congestion points and optimise traffic signal timings, reducing delays and accidents

parts.scheme: 4 marks for each area (very good 4, fair 2). Education: simulate teaching methods or learning environments to find what best improves engagement and performance (e.g. a virtual classroom). Mental wellbeing: simulate factors such as stress, social interactions and lifestyle to predict outcomes and suggest personalised interventions (e.g. anxiety triggers). parts.model: Area 1: Traffic management. Describe: a simulation of cars moving through a town's junctions can show where congestion builds up, and different traffic-light timings can be tested on it to find the one that cuts delays before the real lights are changed. Area 2: Environment. Describe: a climate model can simulate how emissions affect temperatures and flooding, so the effect of different policies can be predicted and the best one chosen.

idea.title: Test it on a model
idea.text: A simulation lets you try changes on a model of a system and see what happens, faster, cheaper and more safely than in real life. Then you make the change that gives the best outcome.

steps.say: Pick two areas you can give a concrete example for, e.g. traffic management and the environment.
For each, name the problem (congestion, rising emissions).
Say what the model would simulate and what you would change in it (light timings, emission policies).
Finish with the improved outcome: shorter delays, better policy decisions.

parts.tip: Each description is worth 4 marks: give a problem, how the model is used and the outcome.

parts.q:
A health agency wants to predict how an infectious disease might spread in a school and evaluate different containment strategies.

Describe how agent-based modelling could be used to simulate disease spread in this scenario.
parts.ask: Describe an agent-based model of a disease spreading in a school

points.text: Each student and teacher could be modelled as an agent with attributes (e.g. vaccination, infection rate)
Agents interact in different locations (e.g. classroom, canteen) and the model's rules simulate infection spread (e.g. contact duration, mask-wearing)

parts.scheme: Very good description 3 marks, fair 2: each student and teacher is modelled as an agent with attributes (e.g. vaccination, infection rate); agents interact in different locations (classroom, canteen) and the model's rules simulate infection spread (contact duration, mask-wearing).
parts.model: Each student and teacher would be an agent with attributes such as infected or not, vaccinated or not, and their timetable. The agents move between classrooms, the canteen and corridors, and when they meet, rules based on contact time, distance and mask-wearing decide whether the infection passes on. Running the simulation shows how the disease spreads through the school.

idea.title: Agent-based models
idea.text: An agent-based model simulates many individuals (agents), each with its own attributes and simple rules for how it behaves and interacts. The overall pattern comes out of all those interactions.

steps.say: Agents: make every student and teacher an agent.
Attributes: give each one properties, e.g. infected, vaccinated, wears a mask.
Interactions: the agents move between locations (classrooms, the canteen) and meet each other.
Rules: each meeting has a chance of passing on the infection, depending on contact time, masks and so on. Run it to watch the disease spread.

parts.q: Outline one emergent behaviour that could be revealed by this simulation.
parts.ask: Give one emergent behaviour the simulation might reveal

points.text: Clusters of infection forming in areas with high interaction, like hallways
Clusters of infection associated with a specific activity, e.g. sports or music
Patterns showing higher infection rates among specific people or age groups (superspreaders)
Recovery leading to patterns such as slowing transmission rates or the end of an outbreak

parts.scheme: Very good description 2 marks, fair 1, for one of: clusters of infection where interaction is high (e.g. hallways); clusters linked to a specific activity (sport, music); higher infection rates among specific people or age groups (superspreaders); recovery leading to slowing transmission or the end of the outbreak; any other valid emergent behaviour.
parts.model: Clusters of infection could form in crowded places like the corridors and the canteen, even though no rule in the model mentions clusters: they emerge from many individual contacts.

idea.title: Emergent behaviour
idea.text: Emergent behaviour is an overall pattern that appears from many agents following simple rules, without anyone programming that pattern in directly.

steps.say: Emergent means a big pattern that no single rule describes: it comes out of many interactions.
Ask what patterns would show up across the whole school: where and in whom infections bunch up, and how the outbreak rises and falls.
Describe one, e.g. clusters of infection in crowded corridors at break time.

parts.q: Suggest one strategy the health agency could test in the model to reduce infection rates and explain how you would measure its success.
parts.ask: Suggest one strategy to test, and how you would measure its success

points.text: Measures to reduce crowding, e.g. social distancing, staggered lunch breaks, quarantine
Mask wearing
Vaccination/booster campaigns
Regular testing/contact tracing
Increased hygiene
Enhanced air ventilation systems
Compare infection rates before and after the strategy
Analyse the time it takes for the disease to stop spreading

parts.scheme: Strategy 2 marks: measures to reduce crowding (social distancing, staggered lunch breaks, quarantine), mask wearing, vaccination or booster campaigns, regular testing or contact tracing, increased hygiene, better air ventilation, or another valid strategy. Measuring success 4 marks (very good 4, fair 2): compare infection rates before and after the strategy; analyse how long it takes the disease to stop spreading.
parts.model: Strategy: staggered lunch breaks, so fewer students are in the canteen at once. Explain: run the simulation with and without the staggered breaks and compare the number of infected students over the same period; the strategy works if infections are lower and the outbreak ends sooner.

idea.title: Run it both ways
idea.text: A simulation is a safe place to test a strategy: run it once without the change and once with it, keeping everything else the same, then compare the results.

steps.say: Pick a strategy that changes the model's rules or attributes: masks, vaccination, fewer people in one place at a time.
Run the simulation without the strategy to get a baseline.
Run it again with the strategy, keeping everything else the same.
Measure success: compare the number or rate of infections, and how long it takes until the spread stops.
